Fruitful
FROOT-ful
adj.
From fruit plus -ful. Webster 1828: producing fruit in abundance; prolific; fertile. In the Authorized Version the word belongs first to a blessing and a command given at creation and repeated after the flood, and then to the patriarchal promises and their fulfilment.

Biblical Definition

Fruitful is the first word of blessing God speaks over living creatures, and it is a command as well as a gift. And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas (Genesis 1:22), and the same blessing is given to man. After the flood it is renewed word for word: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth (Genesis 9:1), and pressed again two verses later, be ye fruitful, and multiply; bring forth abundantly in the earth (Genesis 9:7). It then becomes covenant promise: I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee (Genesis 17:6), passed on to Jacob — I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee (Genesis 35:11). Joseph, who lost everything, names his son for it: God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction (Genesis 41:52), and his father blesses him as a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well (Genesis 49:22). Fruitfulness in Scripture is therefore never a mere biological fact. It is a blessing spoken, a command given, and a covenant kept.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FRUITFUL as producing fruit in abundance; prolific; fertile; and figuratively, productive of any good or effect. Scripture uses both, and joins them: a fruitful womb and a fruitful life are alike God’s blessing.

expand to see more

FRUITFUL, a. — Producing fruit in abundance; as a fruitful tree or soil.

Prolific; bearing children; not barren.

Plenteous; abounding in any thing; productive of any good.

Webster’s second sense — not barren — is what Scripture treats as a blessing and its absence as a grief to be prayed over, from Sarah and Hannah to Elisabeth. The Bible never treats children as an inconvenience to be managed.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:22 — "And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth."

Genesis 9:1 — "And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth."

Genesis 17:6 — "And I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee."

Genesis 35:11 — "And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins;"

Genesis 41:52 — "And the name of the second called he Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Ephraim: that is, Fruitful"

Modern Corruption

The blessing is corrupted by an age that treats children as a cost to be minimized and human fruitfulness as a threat to the planet — and, on the other side, by a piety that makes family size a test of faithfulness Scripture never made it.

expand to see more

God speaks be fruitful and multiply as a blessing before He speaks it as a command, and the two are not in competition. That framing is exactly what the contemporary assumption reverses: children are counted first as expense, career interruption, and environmental burden, and only afterward, if at all, as gift. Scripture’s valuation is the opposite and is stated without hedging — Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward (Psalm 127:3). A church that has absorbed the surrounding calculus will find itself unable to say that plainly, and will quietly stop saying it at all. The renewal of the blessing to Noah after the flood is significant on this point: a world newly emptied by judgment is told to fill again.

The corresponding error is to turn a blessing into a measuring stick. Scripture nowhere makes the number of a couple’s children the index of their faith, and it records godly households of every size, along with barrenness borne by Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elisabeth without any suggestion that their faith was deficient. Joseph’s naming of Ephraim points to the wider sense the New Testament develops: God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Fruitfulness in Christ is bearing much fruit by abiding in the vine (John 15:5), and it is required of every believer, married or single, with children or without.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew verb is parah, to bear fruit or be fruitful, from which Ephraim takes his name; it is paired throughout Genesis with rabah, to multiply or become many.

expand to see more

Hebrew parah (H6509) — to bear fruit, be fruitful; the creation blessing (Genesis 1:22), the Noahic renewal (Genesis 9:1), the patriarchal promise (Genesis 17:6; 35:11).

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to become many, multiply; the constant partner of parah in the formula.

Hebrew Ephraim (H669) — from the same root parah; Joseph names the son for God’s having made him fruitful in affliction (Genesis 41:52).

Hebrew peri (H6529) — fruit; the fruit of the womb (Psalm 127:3) and the fruit of the ground use the same noun.

Greek karpophoreo (G2592) — to bear fruit; the New Testament extension to holiness and good works (Colossians 1:10).

Usage

"Be fruitful, and multiply (Genesis 1:22) — spoken as blessing before it is heard as command."

"I will make thee exceeding fruitful (Genesis 17:6) — the promise to Abraham, kept in a nation and finally in a Seed."

"God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction (Genesis 41:52) — fruitfulness given where it was least expected."
